An assignment must carry a statement of maximum principal indebtedness for Tennessee recording tax purposes.

What state tax applies to a Robertson County sale?

The state conveyance tax runs $3.70 on every $1,000 of value, the same as $0.37 per $100, and the Register collects it under T.C.A. 67-4-409 at the time of recording.

On a $300,000 sale, 300 times $3.70 gives $1,110 in state tax. Add the $1.00 register's fee, and for a three page deed another $15.00 plus the $2.00 processing charge. Loans are taxed separately at $1.15 per $1,000 of debt, with $2,000 left out of the calculation, so a $240,000 mortgage carries $273.70.

The statute exempts certain transfers, among them conveyances between spouses that create or end a tenancy by the entirety, deeds that carry out a will, moves into and out of a revocable living trust, and divorce settlement deeds. A quitclaim is taxed only on the consideration actually paid. Your closing agent can tell you which treatment fits your deed.

How do I file or search records in Robertson County?

Walk a paper original to the counter or send the file electronically. The office says its internet records start January 1, 1998, and it directs searchers to ustitlesearch.com.

  • Electronic recording: accepted through Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and ePN (eRecording Partners).
  • Paper filing: bring the original to the office during business hours along with payment.
  • Preparer details: state law requires a preparer's name and address on every document except releases and charters.
  • Drafting: a title company or lawyer should prepare the deed ahead of your visit.

For a full ownership history on an older parcel, a title company is the usual route.

What happens at the Assessor after a Robertson County deed is recorded?

The Assessor of Property gets a copy of the recorded deed the following day. Putting the buyer's name on the parcel takes roughly 90 days, and until then the next tax notice follows the name on file for January 1.

Sellers should plan for that gap, because the current year's bill may still show your name after closing. The Assessor says the closing papers should spell out who pays for that year, and the address printed on the deed is what the office uses for the following year's notice. The Assessor works at 521 S. Brown St. in Springfield, 615-384-4311. The Trustee, at 515 S. Brown St., 615-384-4238, supplies tax payoffs.

How do the Register, Assessor and Trustee fit together in a Robertson County sale?

Each office owns one link, and a sale touches all three in order. The deed reaches the Register first, the Assessor sees it the next day, and the Trustee collects whatever tax is owed.

  • Before closing: call the Trustee for the balance on each parcel you own, because deeds are indexed under varied spellings and a name search alone can miss one.
  • At closing: state tax and recording charges are collected by the Register, and any open tax is settled with the Trustee.
  • After closing: the Assessor updates the owner name, and the address on the deed drives next year's bill.

A bill that reaches one year delinquent moves to Robertson County Chancery Court, 615-384-5650, and a suit is filed for the tax. Ask the Trustee which stage your bill is in before choosing a closing day.

What does the Robertson County housing profile look like for sellers?

The Census Bureau counts 28,255 households for 2020 to 2024, averaging 2.65 people, and 89.8 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier.

  • Median monthly owner costs: $1,656 with a mortgage and $507 without one.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 823.
  • Average commute: 30.7 minutes, and 87.4 percent of households have a broadband subscription.
  • Education and age: 22.4 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and 17.0 percent of people are 65 or older.

Springfield anchors the county, and Adams, Cedar Hill, Cross Plains, Greenbrier and Orlinda also file through the same Register.

How can Robertson County owners guard against deed fraud?

The Register promotes My Land Alert, a service with free monitoring and notification, no contract and email privacy. Sign up at mylandalert.com to get a message when a document is recorded against your name.

Keep the recorded copy of your deed with your closing papers so you can match the instrument number the Register assigned.

More questions about Robertson County, TN Register of Deeds

What is the minimum Robertson County deed recording fee?

$12.00 before tax: a $10.00 minimum charge plus the $2.00 processing fee. Longer deeds pay $5.00 per page, and a $1.00 register's fee is added when state tax is collected.

What is the Robertson County deed tax rate?

The state conveyance tax is $3.70 per $1,000 of value. Mortgages are taxed at $1.15 per $1,000 once the first $2,000 is set aside.

Does the Robertson County Register accept electronic filings?

Yes. Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners are listed. Paper originals are accepted at the counter during business hours.

How far back do Robertson County online deed records go?

Internet records begin January 1, 1998, searchable through ustitlesearch.com. For anything earlier, ask the Register's staff.

How long until a buyer appears on the Robertson County tax rolls?

About 90 days after the Assessor gets the recorded deed copy, which arrives the day after recording. The bill goes to the January 1 name until the next year.

Williamson County by the numbers

Where does the Williamson County Register of Deeds record a deed?

The Williamson County Register of Deeds is at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, in Franklin, TN 37064. The mailing address is P. O. Box 808, Franklin, TN 37065, the phone number is 615-790-5706, and the office takes questions at register@williamsoncounty-tn.gov. Counter hours run Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and the elected Register is Sherry Anderson.

The office keeps the public record of deeds, deeds of trust, powers of attorney, plats, liens, judgments, wills and similar instruments. Its own site ties that duty to T.C.A. 66-24-101. A deed that never reaches this office stays invisible to a title search, so the recording step matters even on a quick sale.

Several other county desks sit in the same building on West Main Street. The County Clerk is in Suite 135, the Trustee in Suite 203 and the Property Assessor in Suite 300, which makes it simple to settle a records question and a tax question on one trip.

What is Williamson County like for a home seller?

Williamson County is a Middle Tennessee county of about 584 square miles, created by the General Assembly on October 26, 1799 from part of Davidson County. Franklin is the county seat and the largest city, and the county also holds Brentwood, Fairview, Spring Hill (partly in Maury County), Nolensville and Thompson's Station. The Harpeth River and the Little Harpeth River are the main streams.

The county counted 247,726 residents in the 2020 census and an estimated 272,061 in 2025, up from 183,182 in 2010. That census count included 91,133 housing units, and 78.5% of occupied homes were owner occupied. Williamson County Schools operates 50 schools, with a slice of Franklin served by the Franklin Special School District for grades K to 8.

Growth has been steady since the interstate era tied the county to Nashville, so most sales here involve a recorded deed of trust being released and a new one being filed. The Register's office handles both sides of that paperwork.

Which recordation taxes apply to a Williamson County deed?

Tennessee charges two recordation taxes, and the Register of Deeds collects them at filing and remits them to the Department of Revenue. The realty transfer tax is owed by the grantee on a transfer of real property. The indebtedness tax applies to a recorded deed of trust or mortgage.

Tennessee recordation taxes collected at the Williamson County Register of Deeds
TaxRateApplies to
Realty transfer tax37 cents per $100, generally on the greater of price paid or property valueDeeds and other transfer instruments
Indebtedness (mortgage) tax$0.115 per $100 of debt, after the first $2,000Deeds of trust, mortgages, financing statements

Source: Tennessee Department of Revenue, recordation tax overview, citing Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409.

As arithmetic, a $500,000 purchase carries $1,850 in transfer tax at 37 cents per $100. A $400,000 loan carries $457.70 in indebtedness tax, since the first $2,000 is excluded. Your closing agent will show the exact lines on the settlement statement.

What recording fees does the Williamson County office charge?

The office posts a fee calculator on its ProAccess system. You choose the instrument type, enter the page count, and the screen returns a recording fee, a register's fee, a DP fee and an archive fee, followed by a total due. Using the calculator is better than guessing, because the total moves with the number of pages.

The instrument list is long. It includes deed, quitclaim deed, trustee's deed, installment deed, deed of trust, release, plat, easement, lis pendens, power of attorney and last will and testament. Most home sales touch three of those: the warranty or quitclaim deed, the release of the seller's old deed of trust, and the buyer's new deed of trust.

Fees for the same instrument can change when the county or state adjusts them, so rely on the calculator for the day you file. Ask the Register's staff at 615-790-5706 if a document type is unusual.

How can I file documents with the Williamson County Register of Deeds?

You can file at the counter in Franklin or send documents through an electronic recording partner. The office lists four approved e-recording services on its site.

  • CSC (cscglobal.com)
  • ERecording Partners Network (goepn.com)
  • Indecomm Global Services (indecomm.com)
  • Simplifile (simplifile.com)

Title companies and lenders normally submit through one of these channels. A private seller closing without a title company can still bring the signed, notarized deed to the counter, along with payment for the fee total and the transfer tax.

The office also publishes a fraud alert subscription, TitleSearcher for searching records, and Pro Access for professional account holders. If you want to know whether anyone has recorded something against your parcel, a name search on those tools is a good habit before listing.

Which release and correction forms does the office provide?

The office posts downloadable forms for the documents sellers most often need after a payoff. Using the county's own version keeps the filing format right.

  • Notice of Completion
  • Release of Judgment
  • Release of Lien
  • Release of Trust Deed
  • Request for redaction of a Social Security number or military discharge information

A release of trust deed is the document that clears your old mortgage from the record after payoff. If a lender never recorded one, a clean title search will show it, and your title agent can chase it before the sale date. The redaction forms help owners whose Social Security number or military discharge papers sit in a public image.

How do Williamson County property taxes interact with a sale?

Williamson County tax bills are mailed in early October and are payable from the first Monday in October through February 28 of the following year. Partial payments are accepted. On March 1, interest begins at 1.5%, accruing the first of each month, and the Trustee has no authority to waive, prorate or release any piece of the tax or interest.

The tax year covers January 1 through December 31, and bills go to the owner of record as of January 1. If you sell, you must forward the bill to the new owner, and the contract or the title company normally sets who covers what share at closing. The Trustee is at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 203, phone 615-790-5709. The Assessor handles value questions at 615-790-5708.

For an unpaid bill, ask the Trustee for the amount due on your parcel before the contract date. That figure lets the closing agent pay the county from your proceeds in one step.

What should I do before a Williamson County deed is recorded?

A short checklist prevents most recording delays. Gather these items first and confirm them with your closing agent.

  • Order a title search so liens and old deeds of trust surface early.
  • Confirm the Trustee has no balance on the parcel for the current tax year.
  • Have every signature notarized with the notary block filled in completely.
  • Run the fee calculator with the real page count so the check or wire amount is right.
  • Decide whether the closing will file in person or through one of the four e-recording partners.

After recording, the office stamps the instrument with its book and page reference. Keep the recorded copy with your closing file, because lenders and buyers ask for it years later.

More questions about Williamson County, TN Register of Deeds

Who pays the transfer tax on a Williamson County sale?

The grantee, meaning the buyer, owes the realty transfer tax under Tennessee's recordation tax rules. The rate is 37 cents per $100, generally measured on the greater of the price or the property's value. Contracts sometimes shift the cost, so check your sales agreement.

What are the Williamson County Register of Deeds office hours?

The counter is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, Franklin. Call 615-790-5706 to confirm hours around holidays. Electronic recording partners accept submissions outside counter hours.

Can I record a deed in Williamson County without a title company?

Yes. You can bring a signed, notarized deed to the Register's office and pay the fees shown on the calculator plus the transfer tax. A title search beforehand still helps, since it exposes liens that would follow the property.

Does the Register of Deeds collect property taxes?

No. Property taxes are paid to the Williamson County Trustee at Suite 203 of the same building, phone 615-790-5709. The Register only collects the recordation taxes and recording fees that apply when an instrument is filed.

What happens to my property tax bill if I sell in Williamson County?

Bills go to the owner of record as of January 1, and the seller must pass the bill to the new owner. The county will not prorate or waive interest, so the contract and closing statement decide the split. Ask the Trustee for the balance before closing.

Bedford County by the numbers

Where is the Bedford County Register of Deeds in Shelbyville?

The office is at 100 West Side Square, Suite 303, Shelbyville, TN 37160. The phone number is (931) 684-5719 and the fax line is (931) 685-2086, both from the county's contact page.

The county's register of deeds page describes the office as the keeper of records that give public notice of property ownership, liens and contracts. It also says the office earns revenue from recording and filing fees and from a commission on the state conveyance and mortgage taxes it collects, and that it reports the taxes it collects to the state each month.

Two services on that page help sellers. One is an online fee calculator for anyone planning to record documents. The other is a free fraud alert sign-up that notifies a person of property transfers recorded under their name, and an owner can enroll several versions of a name, such as a nickname or a suffix. Anyone who owns a house they rarely visit, such as an inherited property, may find the alert worth setting up.

What should a home seller know about Bedford County?

Bedford County lies in the southern part of Middle Tennessee. It was created in 1807 from Rutherford County and was once the state's largest county by area, though Coffee, Moore, Lincoln and Marshall counties were later carved from it. Today it covers 475 square miles, with Shelbyville as the county seat and only city, and with Bell Buckle, Normandy and Wartrace as towns. Interstate 24, U.S. 231, U.S. 41A and a string of state routes cross it, and the county is part of the Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro combined statistical area.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts give a current picture:

  • 55,273 residents in July 2025, a 10.0% rise from the April 2020 base
  • 21,876 housing units, 71.9% of them owner-occupied
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes of $281,200 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent of $1,051 and median household income of $67,225
  • 378 building permits in 2025
  • Transportation and warehousing receipts of about $1.24 billion in 2022

How is the Tennessee transfer tax figured on a Bedford County deed?

Tennessee's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100, and the buyer pays it to the register when the deed is recorded. The tax base depends on the kind of deed. A quick comparison from the Department of Revenue's recordation tax manual:

Deed typeTax base
Warranty deed or other freehold transferThe greater of the consideration or the property's value at transfer
Quitclaim deedThe consideration given, unless the wording shows an intent to convey the property itself
Warranty deed with a retained life estateFair market value minus the value of the life estate
Modified or amended deedNeeds the book and page of the earlier deed so the register can see the original tax was paid

Language such as "to have and to hold" or "in fee simple" can push a quitclaim deed onto the fair market value basis. The manual's life estate example involves a 70-year-old father who transfers a $250,000 property and keeps a life estate. The deed preparer works out the life estate value, subtracts it, and the tax base falls to $146,765, which yields $543.03 at the 2018 factors used in that example.

At the county's median home value of $281,200, the tax on an ordinary sale would be about $1,040.44. A real sale is taxed on its actual price or value.

What does the oath of value mean for a Bedford County sale?

The buyer, the buyer's agent or a trustee acting for the buyer states under oath, on the face of the deed and in the register's presence, the actual consideration or the value of the property, whichever is greater. The oath is not required when the transfer is exempt. A false statement made knowingly is punishable as perjury.

The Department of Revenue accepts the tax base shown at the local assessor's office as fair market value, or a recent appraisal that the assessor's office has accepted. Anything below that is open to audit, with penalties and interest. The department also reviews recorded deeds from counties it picks at random and compares the value claimed under oath with the assessor value on the Comptroller's website, then may send an inquiry letter to the owner on the deed.

Two rules help avoid double payment. A person who gets several deeds for the same transfer of one parcel pays the tax once, and no tax is due until title actually passes by deed.

The manual lists transfers that owe no realty transfer tax. Among them:

  • A deed by an executor carrying out a will
  • A domestic settlement decree or deed between divorcing parties
  • A release of a life estate to the remainder beneficiaries
  • A transfer to or from a revocable living trust by the same transferor or that person's spouse

What changes when the buyer takes out a mortgage in Bedford County?

A deed of trust adds a separate mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of indebtedness, with the first $2,000 exempt. The borrower pays it, and the register cannot record the instrument until it is paid. Every recorded instrument showing a debt must state "Maximum principal indebtedness for Tennessee recording tax purposes is $___."

An assumption agreement matters if a buyer takes over a seller's loan. If the seller stays liable on the old debt, the manual says no new indebtedness tax is due. If the buyer signs a new contract with the lender and the seller's obligation is cancelled, tax is due on the new mortgage. A holder who does not pay the indebtedness tax owes a penalty of $250 or double the unpaid tax, whichever is greater.

Liens filed by contractors, subcontractors, laborers and mechanics, and judgment liens, are not subject to the mortgage tax. That does not remove them from the title, so a seller should ask the title company to search for them.

Which Bedford County offices handle property tax?

The Property Assessor is on the third floor of the courthouse annex at 100 West Side Square, Suite 301, phone (931) 684-6390. The office values all real and business personal property, keeps the tax maps and prepares the tax rolls for the trustee and municipalities. An owner who thinks the value is wrong appeals to the local board of equalization first and then to the State Board of Equalization.

The Trustee is on the first floor of the annex at 100 Public Square West, Suite 102, phone (931) 684-4303, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. In January and February the office also opens Saturdays from 8 a.m. to noon for tax payments. The trustee takes online payments through a link on the county page and administers the Tax Relief Program, which has existed since 1976 and serves homeowners 65 or older, disabled homeowners and permanently disabled veterans.

Statewide dates apply to Bedford County. Property is assessed as of January 1, current taxes are due the first Monday in October, and the prior year's taxes go delinquent on March 1. A seller with a pending sale should confirm the tax status with the trustee before closing. Tax year 2026 bills have been payable since the first Monday in October, and under the state schedule the last day to pay without interest falls at the end of February.

Ashland City is the county seat, and Kingston Springs, Pegram and Pleasant View are the other incorporated places. The county government site lists these four municipalities.

What does the Cheatham County Register of Deeds do and not do?

The Register records legal instruments, mostly those that transfer title to land, and keeps the public index. Tennessee Code section 8-13-108 lists many of the duties, and other statutes add more.

  • The office cannot prepare, change or revise a deed. State law bars the staff from practicing law, so a seller or buyer should use an attorney or a title company for that step.
  • It cannot run a title search. The staff will help you see which recorded instruments might be liens, but a title company or attorney does the actual search.

Every transfer of real estate in Tennessee carries a state realty transfer tax of 37 cents per $100, figured on the larger of the price paid or the property's value. Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409 puts it inside the recordation tax, which reaches recorded debt as well, such as a deed of trust, at 11.5 cents per $100 once the first $2,000 is set aside.

Take the county's $338,700 median home value from the 2020 to 2024 Census Bureau survey. A sale at that figure carries about $1,253 in transfer tax. Property tax belongs to the Trustee, and values belong to the Assessor, so the Register's counter is the wrong place for either question. Under the Trustee's rule, whoever owns the parcel on January 1 is responsible for that year's tax. A sale contract can shift the cost between buyer and seller, but the Trustee keeps no record of such contracts and tells anyone who buys or sells during the year to verify that the tax is paid, bill or no bill.

At the Trustee's office, the 2026 bill is interest free through Friday, February 26, 2027, while banks accept current-year payments through February 28, 2027. Each month after that adds 1.5 percent. Real property stays with the Trustee until it is a full year delinquent, then goes to the delinquent tax attorney and a Chancery Court suit between March 16 and March 31. Call (615) 792-4298 for the amount on a specific parcel.

The Trustee's office is in Suite A at 354 Frey Street, with hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday and Wednesday, 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday and Thursday, and 8 a.m. to noon Friday. Because deeds are recorded under varied spellings, the Trustee advises owners to track every parcel bought or sold in the year, and a seller should bring the bill to the closing.

The Assessor of Property, in Suite B at the same address, relies on the deeds the Register records. The Assessor's brochure says the primary tool for value is comparing what similar properties sell for, using the hundreds of sales recorded each year by the Register of Deeds. A deed you record therefore becomes a data point in a later reappraisal.

The brochure says Cheatham County is on a five year reappraisal cycle, and gives 2019 as the last reappraisal before its printing. Contact the Assessor at (615) 792-5371 for the current reappraisal year. An owner who disputes a value talks to the Assessor first, and the county Board of Equalization starts hearing cases in June. Cheatham County sits in Middle Tennessee as part of the Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin metropolitan area. The General Assembly created it in 1856 from parts of Davidson, Dickson, Montgomery and Robertson counties, and it was named for state legislator Edward Saunders Cheatham.

The county covers about 302 square miles of land. The Cumberland River crosses it from northwest to southeast with Ashland City on its northern bank, the Harpeth River winds through the hilly south, and Pleasant View sits just south of Interstate 24 on the northern edge. Kingston Springs sits mostly north of Interstate 40, and Pegram lies along U.S. Route 70.

The Census Bureau estimated 42,778 residents in July 2025 and 18,310 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 it reports 16,279 households, median household income of $89,852 and a mean commute of 33.5 minutes. Owners occupy 81.5 percent of homes, which is high, and median gross rent is $1,345. Builders took out 285 permits in 2025.

The office's own FAQ says the staff will not draw up a deed, because a deed is a legal document and an attorney should prepare it. It also will not run a title search to tell you about liens, though the indexes are on public computers for anyone to use.

Recording changes the name on the public record and has no effect on what is owed. Property tax follows the January 1 assessment, comes due on the first Monday of October, and turns delinquent once February ends, per the Comptroller's calendar.

Fayette County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Fayette County, TN?

Deeds are recorded at the Fayette County Register of Deeds in the courthouse at 16755 Highway 64, Suite 108, in Somerville, TN 38068. Mail goes to P.O. Box 99 at the same town, and the phone number is 901-465-5251. The register is an elected official who serves a four-year term, and the county's staff page lists Kim Akins as the current Register.

The office records, indexes and stores real estate and business papers, including deed records, property transfers, mortgages and liens. It does not prepare any of them. The register's FAQ says documents must be ready for recording when they arrive, and staff make no claim about whether a document is legally valid. A seller whose buyer is using a title company rarely has to deal with the counter directly, but it helps to know what the office will and will not do.

What does the Fayette County register's office accept for payment and paperwork?

The office takes cash, a personal or business check with ID, or a money order, and it does not take credit or debit cards. That detail matters for an out-of-town buyer who plans to walk a deed in on closing day.

The FAQ also lays out how paperwork is handled:

  • Only original, signed, notarized documents are recorded, apart from a certified copy of something already recorded in another government office
  • The notary seal goes near the notary's name, after each signature and acknowledgment
  • The deed must show the preparer's name and address, and since April 11, 2012 it may appear anywhere in the document
  • The office returns originals to the person who brought or mailed them and keeps no originals
  • A release of lien is filed by the mortgage company once the loan is paid off

The register will not run a title search for liens or other encumbrances, but staff will check the status of a particular release or assignment if you ask. Wills that were never probated are not kept as recorded documents. A probated will from another county or state may be recorded in Fayette County when the person owned land here.

How much is the Fayette County transfer tax on a sale?

The state realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of the price or value, and the buyer pays it when the deed is recorded. For a sale at the county's median home value of $340,800 from the 2020-2024 Census estimates, the figure comes to $1,260.96.

Transfer tax at $0.37 per $100, illustrated for Fayette County prices

Source: rate from the Tennessee Department of Revenue; median value from Census QuickFacts. The amounts are simple multiplication and your own deed sets the actual figure.

Fayette's register asks for an oath of consideration on every transfer unless the deed cites a Tennessee statute that makes it exempt, such as a divorce or the creation of a tenancy. Staff can later tell anyone the amount sworn on the oath, which is how people find a recorded sale price.

What does a Fayette County deed need so the register accepts it?

Tennessee law sets out what a deed must contain, and the register's job is to check that the paper is acceptable, not to judge its legal effect. The checklist drawn from the University of Tennessee county training guide is short.

  • Legible text and an authenticated signature (T.C.A. 66-24-101 and 66-22-101)
  • Owner and taxpayer names and addresses (66-24-114)
  • A derivation clause pointing to the prior deed (66-24-110)
  • The preparer's name and address (66-24-115)
  • A parcel identification number (66-24-122)
  • Payment of fees and any transfer tax

If you only know an address and not a name, the register's FAQ suggests calling the Fayette County Property Assessor at 901-465-5226 to learn the taxpayer on a parcel, since the deed indexes work by grantor and grantee names. Subdivision plats are held at the office and show lot size, setbacks and easements as recorded, though a plat is no substitute for a survey.

Surveys themselves are not recorded documents. For acreage, the Assessor of Property can supply tax and aerial maps, but the FAQ points out that these are drawn from the description in your deed and are not official surveys. A seller of a rural parcel who is unsure of the lines should hire a surveyor before signing a contract with acreage figures in it.

What is Fayette County like for a home seller?

Fayette County lies east of Memphis and is part of the Memphis metropolitan area. Its seat is Somerville, and the county covers 706 square miles, the third largest in Tennessee by area. The county website lists eleven municipalities: Braden, Gallaway, Grand Junction, Hickory Withe, La Grange, Moscow, Oakland, Piperton, Rossville, Somerville and Williston.

The county was created by the Tennessee General Assembly in 1824 from parts of Shelby and Hardeman counties and was named for the Marquis de la Fayette, and Somerville was chosen as its seat that same year. The two-century-old county has a long recorded land history, and the register can tell you the date, volume and page of any deed it holds.

Growth has shifted west. Since Highway 64 was widened to four lanes in the early 1990s, Oakland has grown past the county seat in population as people who work in Shelby County look for cheaper housing. Agriculture is still the base of the county economy.

Census QuickFacts for the county give a sense of the market:

  • 45,071 residents in the July 2025 estimate, an 8.0 percent rise from the 2020 base
  • 81.4 percent of homes owner-occupied, with a median gross rent of $902
  • Median household income of $88,456
  • 25.4 percent of residents are 65 or older, and the mean commute is 34.1 minutes
  • 356 building permits issued in 2025

What protects a Fayette County owner from deed fraud?

The register runs a Property Fraud Alert system that notifies owners when something is recorded against their property or business. Sign-up is through a link on the register's services page, and it is a sensible step before you list or sell, because it flags a filing you did not make before it causes trouble.

After a sale, check that the deed and the release of your old deed of trust were both recorded. The register's FAQ explains the mortgage company files the release once you are paid off, and you can request a copy of it. Call 901-465-5251 for the date, volume and page of a recorded document. Staff can also tell you if a release of a deed of trust has been attempted, though they make no legal claim about whether it is accurate.

Property tax is a separate matter from recording. Ask the county trustee and the assessor, whose phone number is 901-465-5226, about the current bill and valuation before the closing date so nothing surprises the title company.

What is the phone number for the Fayette County Register of Deeds?

It is 901-465-5251. The office is in the courthouse at 16755 Highway 64, Suite 108, in Somerville, and mail goes to P.O. Box 99, Somerville, TN 38068.

Can I pay recording fees by credit card in Fayette County?

No. The register accepts cash, a check with ID, or a money order, and states that it does not accept credit or debit cards.

Does the Fayette County register prepare my deed?

No. The office does not draw up documents, and it makes no claim that a document is legally valid. Bring a deed prepared with all filing requirements, signed and notarized.

How do I find who owns a Fayette County parcel if I only have an address?

Call the Fayette County Property Assessor at 901-465-5226. The register's indexes work by name, so the assessor can give the taxpayer for a parcel first.

How much is the transfer tax on a Fayette County house sale?

The buyer pays $0.37 for each $100 of the price. On a $340,800 home, the county's median value in Census data, that is about $1,260.96.

Where does Franklin County, TN keep its deed records?

The register's website describes the job broadly. The office creates and preserves a record of each instrument the law requires or allows to be filed, among them deeds, mortgages, liens and plats, along with leases, wills, court orders and military discharges. Those records give public notice of who owns land and what claims sit against it, and the papers stay in the county seat.

For a house sale, the deed that moves title to your buyer is indexed in Winchester, and so is the paper that releases your old loan.

Which Franklin County offices does a seller deal with?

Three offices share the courthouse at 1 South Jefferson Street, so most of a seller's errands can be done in one trip. The register records, the assessor values, and the trustee collects the tax.

Source: Franklin County Property Assessor, Franklin County Trustee and the Register of Deeds site. The assessor's counter runs weekdays from eight until half past four.

The assessor's office keeps an individual property record card on every parcel in the county, about 25,000 in all. Records are updated weekly through the state's Local Assessor System for web viewing, and a public terminal at the office can pull them up. Before you set an asking price, have the staff read back the owner of record and the property classification.

What transfer tax would a Winchester-area sale carry?

On a transfer of real property the state takes 37 cents for each $100 of the price or value, and the buyer pays it to the register at recording. The 2020-2024 Census estimate puts a typical owned home here at $236,900, which would owe about $876.53.

A mortgage tax of 11.5 cents per $100 of debt applies to new loans after the first $2,000, and the borrower covers it.

Whichever is higher, the price paid or the property's value, sets the tax base, and the buyer swears to it before the register. A deed that cites a statutory exemption skips the oath. The exempt list includes ending a tenancy by the entirety and releasing a life estate to the beneficiaries.

Why might the Franklin County register refuse a deed?

The register checks whether a paper can be accepted and leaves its legal effect to the drafter. The University of Tennessee's county advisory staff lists what a deed needs.

  • Readable text and a notary's acknowledgment (Tennessee Code sections 66-24-101 and 66-22-101)
  • Names and addresses of the owner and the taxpayer, section 66-24-114
  • A derivation clause that cites the prior deed, section 66-24-110
  • The drafter's name and address, section 66-24-115
  • The parcel number, section 66-24-122
  • Fees, plus transfer tax if any is owed, on the day of filing

A document in another language needs a translation attached, and registers may turn away an unreadable page. One missing item sends the deed back, which can push a closing date. Compare the parcel number on the deed with the one on your tax bill before anyone signs.

What is Franklin County like for a home seller?

Franklin County lies on the Alabama line at the eastern boundary of Middle Tennessee. It covers 576 square miles, of which 555 are land, and it climbs from the Nashville Basin over the Highland Rim and onto the Cumberland Plateau, a rise of about 1,300 feet. The county was organized in 1807 and named for Benjamin Franklin, and Winchester is the seat.

The county's own website lists the University of the South at Sewanee, Tims Ford Reservoir and State Park, and a manufacturing base tied to the automotive industry. Wikipedia adds that Nissan built a large engine plant at Decherd and that the Arnold Engineering Development Center lies partly in the county. Cowan, Decherd, Estill Springs, Sewanee, Huntland, Sherwood and Winchester are the communities named on the county site, and Interstate 24 gives access to Chattanooga.

Several early towns gave up their charters in the late nineteenth century. Wikipedia explains that state law then allowed liquor sales only in incorporated places, so towns abolished their charters to stay dry. Today the county site lists seven communities, among them Sherwood, which it describes as an unincorporated community. The county's pages also point to the railroad museum and Mountain Goat Trail at Cowan, golf courses near Decherd, and mineral springs at Estill Springs.

Settlement by white families began around 1800, and in the twentieth century the Tennessee Valley Authority brought flood control, power and new lakes. The same projects displaced residents whose homes were flooded. Wikipedia notes that in the 2020 census the county had 19,395 housing units, 13.3 percent of them vacant, and that about two thirds of residents lived in rural areas.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts put numbers on the housing picture:

  • 45,579 residents in the July 2025 estimate, up 6.6 percent from the 2020 base
  • 77.4 percent owner-occupied, with a median gross rent of $894
  • Median household income of $63,494 and a median home value of $236,900
  • 22.5 percent of residents are 65 or older
  • 323 building permits issued in 2025

Median household income here is below the $75,003 of neighboring Dickson County and the $88,456 of Fayette County in the same Census table.

What do Franklin County owners need to know about the tax calendar?

Under the Comptroller's schedule the assessment date is January 1. Bills fall due the first Monday in October, and February 28 is the final day to pay with no interest. Balances are delinquent from March 1.

State law makes the assessor responsible for locating and identifying every taxable property in Franklin County, appraising it and setting its assessed value. The trustee bills and collects but has no say over the appraisal, so a complaint about value goes to the assessor first. The assessor says the commission sets the rate.

The Comptroller's tax calculator says a home is assessed at a quarter of its appraised value. For a $236,900 house that is $59,225, and the tax is that figure divided by 100 and multiplied by the rate. Ask the trustee for the current rate and balance.

Challenges go first to the board of equalization for the county, which convenes June 1. Elderly or disabled owners with 2025 income of $38,470 or less may qualify for state relief, and the form goes to the trustee within 35 days after the delinquency date.

At the Register of Deeds, 1 South Jefferson Street in Winchester, TN 37398. Call (931) 967-2840. The register is Nancy K. Ringer, and the office is in the county seat.

Who do I call to check my Franklin County property tax?

Call the Franklin County Trustee at (931) 967-2962. The trustee collects the tax, while the Property Assessor at (931) 967-3869 handles the appraisal and assessment.

How many parcels does the Franklin County assessor track?

About 25,000. The assessor keeps a property record card on each parcel, updated weekly through the state's Local Assessor System for web viewing.

About $876.53. Tennessee charges $0.37 per $100 of the price or value, and the buyer pays it when the deed is recorded.

The county website names Cowan, Decherd, Estill Springs, Sewanee, Huntland, Sherwood and Winchester, with Winchester as the county seat. Sewanee is home to the University of the South.

What does the Hamblen County Register of Deeds handle?

This office is where a sale becomes part of the public record. When a Morristown house changes hands, the deed is presented here, receives a book and page reference, and joins the chain of title that every later buyer, lender and title searcher will read. Staff also record deeds of trust, releases of paid-off loans, powers of attorney, charters, plats and military discharges.

Records on file go back to 1860. The office is scanning deeds and plats into digital form for the years since 1978, so ask staff how to search for anything older.

Two state taxes pass through the counter as well, the realty transfer tax on land sales and the mortgage tax on debt. The Tennessee Department of Revenue requires every register to collect them, and on a typical sale they come to far more than the filing fee.

Where is the Register of Deeds office, and what should I bring?

Look for the third floor of the Administrative Building at the Hamblen County Courthouse, 511 West Second North Street, Morristown, TN 37814. The telephone is 423-586-6551 and the fax line is 423-318-2505.

The county covers 176 square miles, 161 of them land, and the courthouse sits in Morristown, the seat. Census QuickFacts counts 68,843 people, 28,945 housing units and 258 building permits for 2025, and puts typical owner-occupied value at $210,900.

Plan your visit around this short list:

  • The signed deed, with the grantee or an agent prepared to swear to the price or value in front of the Register
  • Parcel details from the Assessor, who works in the same building on 423-586-1852
  • For an amended deed, the book and page of the earlier recorded version
  • Funds for the filing fee and the tax

What are the filing charges at the Hamblen County Register of Deeds?

Tennessee sets recording fees by statute, so every county charges the same amounts. The numbers below come from the University of Tennessee county assistance service's summary of a register's standard fees. Military discharges are filed at no charge.

ItemFeeSource
Standard document, up to two pages$10.00UT CTAS, Standard Fees

Take a four-page deed. Page charges add up to $20, the data processing charge is $2 and the tax receipt is $1, so the filing side is $23. Pages cannot exceed 8 1/2 by 14 inches.

What tax does a buyer owe when a Hamblen County deed is recorded?

The realty transfer tax is 37 cents on each $100 of price, or 0.37 percent. The Department of Revenue applies it to whichever figure is greater: the price paid, or what the parcel is worth on the transfer date. State law makes the grantee on the deed responsible, and payment is taken by the register in the county where the instrument is presented.

Try the arithmetic at the county's typical home value. At $210,900 there are 2,109 hundreds, and 2,109 times $0.37 gives $780.33. Adding the $23 filing charges for the four-page deed from the table takes the counter total to $803.33. How that sum is shared appears on your closing statement.

The deed has to carry a sworn statement of the actual consideration or value, made in the Register's presence. A knowingly false statement is punishable as perjury. A buyer who holds several deeds for one and the same parcel pays the tax only once, and no tax comes due until title actually passes by deed. The state also samples recorded deeds now and then, setting the sworn value beside the assessor's figure, and a mismatch may bring a letter. It accepts either the assessor's tax base or a recent appraisal that the assessor's office has accepted as the fair market value.

Which transfers in Hamblen County owe no transfer tax?

The Revenue Department's manual lists these among the transfers that escape the tax:

  • Conveyances between spouses, or ones that create or end an entireties tenancy
  • A deed signed by an executor to carry out a will
  • Transfers made under a divorce decree or domestic settlement
  • Moves of a home into a revocable living trust by its creator or the creator's spouse, and back out
  • Distributions by a trustee to beneficiaries under a will or revocable trust
  • Any transfer to or from a government body

An exempt transfer needs no oath. Quitclaim deeds get a closer look from the state. Tax is figured on the consideration given, unless the wording shows an intent to convey the property itself, as phrases like to have and to hold or in fee simple do. If that language appears, market value controls instead.

How does the mortgage tax work at the Hamblen County Register of Deeds?

Whenever a deed of trust or similar debt instrument is recorded, an indebtedness tax applies at $0.115 per $100 of debt, and the first $2,000 is left out. The borrower pays it to the Register along with the filing charges.

A buyer financing $168,000 is taxed on $166,000, which comes to $190.90. The instrument must state, on its face or in a sworn attachment, the maximum principal indebtedness for Tennessee recording tax purposes. The register may not record it until that statement is present and payment has been made. A holder who skips or underpays the debt tax owes a penalty of $250 or double the unpaid amount, whichever is larger.

Loan assumptions fall into two groups. When the buyer promises to pay the seller's debt while the seller stays liable, no new tax arises, because the debt is not new. When the buyer signs a fresh contract with the lender that cancels the seller's duty, the new mortgage carries the tax.

How can I research a deed or parcel in Hamblen County?

Begin with Assessor of Property Keith Ely, who works in the same courthouse. His office keeps ownership, address, deed references and appraised value for roughly 32,000 parcels and maintains more than 400 maps showing lot lines and acreage. Take the book and page number from that record to the Register to read the recorded instrument itself.

Certified copies cost $1 a page. The scanning project covers 1978 forward, so ask the staff how to search for earlier records.

If you plan a quick sale, have the title company pull the chain of title early. An unrecorded deed, a missing release on an old loan, or a name that differs between the deed and the tax roll can hold up a closing.

More questions about Hamblen County, TN Register of Deeds

Where is the Hamblen County Register of Deeds located?

On the third floor of the Administrative Building at the courthouse, 511 West Second North Street, Morristown, TN 37814. The phone number is 423-586-6551.

How much does the Hamblen County Register of Deeds charge to file a deed?

Ten dollars covers up to two pages, with $5 for each added page, plus $2 for data processing and $1 for the tax receipt. The state's $0.37 per $100 transfer tax comes on top.

Which party is responsible for transfer tax on a Hamblen County sale?

The buyer named in the deed carries the legal duty, and the Register takes payment when the deed is filed. Your closing statement shows how the two sides handled it. The levy is 37 cents per $100.

Do any Hamblen County deeds skip the transfer tax?

Yes. Transfers between spouses, an executor's deed carrying out a will, divorce decree transfers and moves into a revocable living trust are among those the state exempts.

Does the Register of Deeds keep property tax records?

No. Values and tax rolls belong to the Assessor of Property at 423-586-1852, and bills are paid to the Trustee at 423-586-6290. The Register records deeds and collects the state recording taxes.

  • How will the recorded original be returned, and how long does it take?
  • Can a title company record by an electronic method, or does it need to deliver the paper?

The register's answers apply on the day you ask, and fees and forms can change. If you sell as-is to a buyer who pays cash, the deed is usually the only document at the register, so the visit is quick when the paperwork is ready.

How is Rhea County laid out for a seller?

Rhea County covers 336 square miles, of which 21 are water, and its 315 square miles of land held about 104 people per square mile in 2020. Walden Ridge on the Cumberland Plateau forms the western edge. The Tennessee River marks the border with Meigs County in the east, and Whites Creek separates Rhea from Roane County to the north.

Watts Bar Dam crosses the Tennessee River near Spring City. The lake above the dam is Watts Bar Lake, and the lake below it is Chickamauga Lake. The Watts Bar Nuclear Generating Station stands near the dam. U.S. Route 27 is the main north-south road. State Route 30 meets it in Dayton, and State Route 68 links Spring City with Madisonville and Crossville.

Dayton is the county seat and largest town, with Graysville and Spring City as the two towns. Five counties touch Rhea: Cumberland, Roane, Meigs, Hamilton and Bledsoe. State natural areas include Laurel-Snow, Piney Falls and Stringing Fork Falls, and part of the Cumberland Trail runs through the county. The county sits in the Eastern Time Zone, and Bledsoe and Cumberland counties to the west keep Central Time. The Dayton micropolitan area belongs to the Chattanooga-Cleveland-Dalton combined statistical area.

What do Census figures say about Rhea County homes?

The Census Bureau estimates 34,844 residents on July 1, 2025, up 4.8 percent from the April 2020 base. It lists 15,955 housing units and 13,475 households. Owners live in 71.5 percent of occupied homes, and the median owner-occupied value is $206,000 for 2020 to 2024.

Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,326, and owners without one report $365. Median gross rent is $839. Median household income is $55,033, and 14.0 percent of residents are below the poverty line. Workers face a mean commute of 29.5 minutes, the longest of the four Tennessee counties compared in that table. The county issued 151 building permits in 2025.

What history shapes Rhea County today?

Rhea County was founded in 1807 and named for John Rhea, a Tennessee politician and Revolutionary War veteran. A portion of the Trail of Tears crossed the county in the 1830s. The county seat moved from the Washington community to Dayton in 1890 after the Cincinnati-Chattanooga Railroad reached Smith's Crossroads and Chattanooga grew.

The Scopes Trial took place at the Rhea County Courthouse in 1925, and William Jennings Bryan died in Dayton soon after it ended. Statues of Bryan and of defense lawyer Clarence Darrow stand on the courthouse grounds. Bryan College, named for William Jennings Bryan, is in Dayton, Chattanooga State Community College has a small campus there, and Rhea County Schools sends high school students to Rhea County High School in Evensville. Dayton City School serves grades K through 8 inside the city.

More questions about Rhea County, TN Register of Deeds

Where do I record a deed for a house in Rhea County?

At the Rhea County Register of Deeds, 375 Church Street, Suite 106, Dayton, TN 37321. The phone number is 423-775-7841.

How much is the Tennessee transfer tax on a Rhea County sale?

It is $0.37 per $100, generally on the greater of the price paid or the property's value. On a $206,000 sale that comes to $762.20, before the register's own recording fee.

Is there a mortgage tax in Rhea County?

Yes. Tennessee charges $0.115 per $100 of indebtedness when a deed of trust is recorded, and the first $2,000 is exempt. A $180,000 loan owes $204.70.

Who gets my property tax payoff in Rhea County?

The Rhea County Trustee, 375 Church Street, Suite 110, at 423-775-7810. Ask for the open balance and any interest to your closing date, and give it to the title company.

Can I sell my Rhea County house if the deed is still in a parent's name?

A title agent has to resolve who holds title before a buyer can close. Ask the register at 423-775-7841 what the recorded chain of deeds shows, and bring the findings to an attorney or title company.

Tipton County by the numbers

Who records deeds in Tipton County?

Recording is the job of the county's Register of Deeds. Ask the Register of Deeds office for its current mailing address and phone number. The county's own page cites Tennessee Code 66-24-101 for the office's main duty, which is recording deeds and other instruments the law requires or allows to be filed.

The page also lists what can be recorded: deeds, powers of attorney, mortgages, marriage settlements, plats and military discharges. The Register also collects and accounts for the fees and taxes that go with each filing. For a home sale, that normally means the deed from seller to buyer and, when the buyer borrows, the lender's mortgage or deed of trust. Both documents go through the same counter and are charged the fees below. Ask the title company or closing attorney who will deliver the documents to the office.

Call the office before a closing to ask for its current hours and whether it accepts electronic filing. Lookup of property records is separate: the Assessor's parcel search is at tiptontn.geopowered.com/PropertySearch.

Why does the history of Tipton County land matter at a closing?

This is the Mississippi River side of Tennessee, a county seated at Covington and cut from Shelby County in the autumn of 1823. Its roads and rail lines tell the story of how land changed hands. Randolph was Tennessee's busiest shipping point around 1830, the Memphis and Ohio line passed through what is now Mason in December 1855, and tracks reached Covington in July 1873.

The 1811 and 1812 New Madrid earthquakes moved the river and left places like Reverie on the Arkansas side. The county's western boundary still follows the old channel, so land near the river is where boundary history matters most. Other incorporated places include Munford, Atoka, Brighton, Mason, Burlison, Garland and Gilt Edge.

A few numbers from the Census Bureau frame the local market:

  • About 25,000 housing units for roughly 62,000 residents
  • Three of every four households own their home
  • A median owned-home value of $240,600 for 2020 to 2024
  • 91.4% of people stayed in the same house for a year, which points to settled ownership

What are the Tipton County recording charges?

The county lists its recording fees on the Register's page, using the standard Tennessee schedule. An ordinary instrument of one or two pages is $10.00, and each page after the second is $5.00. Add a $2.00 data processing fee per document and a $1.00 clerk's fee whenever state tax is paid.

ItemFeeSource
Instrument of one or two pages$10.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Each additional page after two$5.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Plat$15.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Data processing, per document$2.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Clerk's fee, only when state tax is paid$1.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Certified copy, per page$1.00Tipton County Register of Deeds
Military dischargeNo chargeTipton County Register of Deeds

For a four-page warranty deed on which state tax is paid, the recording charge is $10 for the first two pages, $10 for the next two, $2 for data processing and $1 for the clerk's fee, a total of $23. A release or assignment added to an instrument costs $5.00 for each one after the first, which matters when a payoff and a new loan are recorded together. UCC fixture filings are $13.00, and UCC filings over 10 pages add $0.50 per page.

How much transfer tax and mortgage tax apply in Tipton County?

The Register's counter also collects two state taxes. One is the realty transfer tax, set at 37 cents for each $100 of the price. The other is the mortgage tax at 11.5 cents for each $100 of debt, and the first $2,000 of debt is exempt. The Tennessee Department of Revenue posts the same rates, which the county's fee list labels the conveyance tax and the mortgage tax.

The numbers add up fast on a typical sale. A home sold at the Census median of $240,600 produces a transfer tax of about $890. A $200,000 loan produces a mortgage tax of $227.70, since the taxable amount is $198,000. Both are separate from the recording fees in the table above.

Who pays which tax is set in the purchase contract and shown on the settlement statement, so confirm it with the closing agent before signing. On a $300,000 sale the transfer tax would be $1,110, and a seller who expects a net sheet to the dollar should see that line in advance. County property tax is a separate matter handled by the Trustee, and the Register does not collect it.

Does recording a deed change who gets the next tax notice?

It can. Each October the Trustee mails the notice to whoever held title on January 1. A deed recorded in time for the September cutoff also triggers a second copy to the buyer. A buyer whose deed lands later may see no bill at all and should call the Trustee at 901-476-0211.

That office also posts the numbers a buyer will care about: a 2026 county rate of $1.3417, residential assessment at 25 percent, interest-free payment through February 28, and monthly interest after that. Before a deed goes to the Register, work through this short checklist:

  • Get the Trustee's status on the parcel for the current year
  • Find out whether a city bill, such as Covington's, is also open
  • Check that the legal description and parcel number match the deed
  • Ask the Register's office how it takes payment of the recording fee and state tax

Which Tipton County office holds which record?

The county's "Where Do I" page sorts common requests by office, which helps when a sale turns up a question that is not a recording matter. The Register handles copies of deeds and plats and the recording of a deed or other document. Other pieces of a sale sit elsewhere:

  • Tax maps, property assessment values and the Greenbelt Program: Property Assessor
  • Paying property taxes: Trustee
  • Tax sale auctions: Chancery Court
  • Rezoning and zoning of county properties: Planning and Development
  • Obtaining a new address: TCECD 911

The Assessor also keeps the parcel history. Its page notes that the Assessor tracks property sales, building permits and zoning changes when updating the roll, so a recorded deed feeds into the Assessor's records. A buyer who needs a corrected mailing address for the tax bill should contact the Assessor at 901-476-0213.

What is the property fraud alert, and who should sign up?

The Register offers a free Property Fraud Alert through its computer vendor. Once an owner enrolls, an email arrives whenever a document is recorded under a name the owner has added. A seller who just closed, or an heir managing a family house, can use it to watch for filings under the old owner's name. The enrollment steps on the county's page are:

  • Have a valid email address ready
  • Go to www.mylandalert.com and click Register in the upper left
  • Accept the terms at the bottom of the page and enter the email address
  • Click the verification link, choose a password, and add the names to watch

More questions about Tipton County, TN Register of Deeds

Which office accepts a deed for recording in Tipton County?

It goes to the Register of Deeds in Covington. The office mails to PO Box 626, Covington, TN 38019, and answers deed questions at 901-476-0204.

What fees apply when a Tipton County deed is recorded?

The base charge is $10.00 for up to two pages, with $5.00 for every page beyond that, a $2.00 data processing fee, and a $1.00 clerk's fee whenever state tax is paid.

How big is the state tax on a Tipton County sale?

The state charges $0.37 for each $100 of the price, so a $240,600 sale carries about $890.

Does a Tipton County loan carry its own tax?

Yes. The state mortgage tax is $0.115 for each $100 of debt beyond the first $2,000, which makes a $200,000 loan cost $227.70.

Is there a free warning when something is filed under my name?

Yes. The Register sponsors a free fraud alert at mylandalert.com. Once you enroll a name, an email arrives each time a document is filed under it.
